name: Zoe Hansen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hi Zoe, thanks for joining. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group. We're not linked to AI companies, employers or government, and nothing you say goes out with your name on it. What's a normal working day for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I translate Japanese into English, mostly games and apps, plus subtitles for a couple of streaming clients. That means menus, item descriptions, dialogue for characters, and a lot of puns that don't survive the trip. I work from my studio flat with two monitors and a cat who sits on the keyboard. Most days I'm running a machine draft through my own setup, then rewriting the dialogue so it sounds like a person actually said it.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I've built a little pipeline: the game text goes in, an AI model does a first pass with a glossary of the game's terms, and then I get a spreadsheet with the draft and a note on anything odd. It took me most of last year to get right. I'm quicker than most translators I know, so I take more projects.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like and what wears you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the dialogue, getting a grumpy old blacksmith to sound grumpy in English. What wears me down is crunch, when a studio moves the launch date and suddenly I'm doing 40,000 words in a week.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Good, honestly. I've got about ten months of costs in savings and some shares on top. I rent, I live alone, no kids, so my costs are low and my rates are on the higher side for this work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So the boring outcome. My pipeline just stays a nice little advantage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you it was a tool, not a translator. Online I'd post a thread about how I use it, because people always ask.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's good for me. If the AI tools stop at roughly where they are now, I'm one of the translators who already gets the most out of them. That's a head start that doesn't run out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my clients and tighten the pipeline, maybe add automatic checks for text that's too long for the game's buttons. I'd raise my rates for dialogue-heavy work, since that's where I'm best. I'd probably take a proper holiday in Japan next spring, finally.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Pleased, a little. It's the version where my bet pays off quietly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in this picture that would bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rates for plain app text, the menus and settings screens. Those are already sliding, because studios run them straight through a machine. That's maybe a fifth of my work, so I'd shrug and fill the gap with dialogue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Friends who refuse to touch the tools. My friend Priya from the climbing gym is a UX writer, and she's fine. But I know translators who still do everything by hand, and even in the slow version they're losing jobs to people like me.

say: I'd say AI is a **tool, not a translator**, and post how I use it.
I'd share my **workflow** online because people always ask about it.
think: My **head start** with the tools doesn't run out if AI stalls here.
Plain **app text** is sliding, but it's only about a fifth of my work.
do: Add automatic checks for **text length** to her translation pipeline.
Take a **holiday in Japan** next spring.
feel: **Calm** and a little pleased that her bet pays off quietly.
S0.quote: If the AI tools stop at roughly where they are now, I'm one of the translators who already gets the most out of them.
fieldNote: She already runs her own **AI pipeline**, so a plateau rewards her.
Her concern is for **hand-only translators**, not herself.
She is losing **menu work** but shrugs because dialogue pays better.

steps.text: Add a text-length check for game buttons to her pipeline
Raise rates for dialogue-heavy game projects

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, that's more like what I actually expect.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say translators should stop asking whether to use AI and start asking what part of the job is still theirs. I'd say it at the industry meetup and online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means my advantage shrinks, because everyone gets a pipeline like mine for free. The studios will run the whole game through AI and pay someone to fix the tone. I'd want to be that someone, but there'd be fewer of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sell my pipeline setup as a service to small studios that don't have a localisation team, a few thousand per project. I'd keep the dialogue work and drop the menu jobs entirely. I'd also learn the newer models every few months, the same way I learned the old ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a restless way. I'd rather be early than right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said there'd be fewer of you. Are you worried you won't be one of them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. I'm average at the translating itself, I'm good at the setup around it. If the setup becomes a button, I'm just an average translator with a nice spreadsheet. That's why I'd sell the setup while it's still worth something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much would you need to earn from that side work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Even two small studios a year would replace the menu work I'm dropping. It's not about getting rich. It's about having something that isn't one client sending me 40,000 words in a crunch week.

say: I'd say translators should ask what part of the job is **still theirs**.
I'd say it at the **industry meetup** and online.
think: My **advantage shrinks** once everyone gets a pipeline like mine for free.
Studios will pay someone to **fix the tone**, but fewer people.
do: Sell her **pipeline setup** to small studios for a few thousand per project.
Drop **menu jobs** and keep dialogue work.
Learn each **new model** within months of release.
feel: Uneasy, but **restless**, preferring to be early than right.
S1.quote: If the setup becomes a button, I'm just an average translator with a nice spreadsheet.
fieldNote: She is honest that her edge is the **workflow**, not the translating itself.
She **sells the pipeline** while it's still worth something.
Even here her own income feels **mostly safe**, which keeps her at uneasy.

steps.text: Sell her AI localisation setup to two small studios a year
Stop taking menu and settings-screen jobs
Test each new translation model within months of release

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Oh. Two years. That's the one I joke about at the pub.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should all be honest that translation as a paid job is ending, and I'd say it without drama. Some people would hate me for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record: I'd have maybe 18 good months. All my work is screen work, so the robot delay means nothing to me. My savings would carry me, but I'd need a new career by 30.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a salaried job at a game studio running their AI localisation, because a salary plus my freelance clients lets me save twice as fast. I'd put a chunk of my shares into the AI companies themselves; if they're going to win, I'd rather own a little piece. Then I'd look hard at what people still pay a human for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, and a bit thrilled, which I know is weird.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thrilled?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's the biggest change in my lifetime and I'd be in the middle of it. I'm 27, I live alone, and nobody depends on me, so if I have to be thrown into the deep end, better now than at 50.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you think people would still pay a human for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Being in the room. Hosting fan events, talking to players in Japan and the West, being the face of a game. I don't know if that's a career or a hobby, honestly.

say: I'd say translation as a **paid job** is ending, plainly and without drama.
I'd accept that **some people** would hate me for saying it.
think: I'd have maybe **18 good months**, since all my work is on screen.
Savings carry me, but I'd need a **new career by 30**.
do: Take a **salaried studio job** running AI localisation alongside freelance clients.
Move part of her shares into **AI companies**.
Research what people still pay **a human** for.
feel: **Anxious** and oddly thrilled at being in the middle of it.
S2.quote: I'm 27, I live alone, and nobody depends on me, so if I have to be thrown into the deep end, better now than at 50.
fieldNote: She treats her **youth and low costs** as an advantage in a fast shock.
She hedges by **owning AI shares**, a pragmatic rather than angry response.
She isn't sure **being in the room** is a career or a hobby.

steps.text: Take an in-house studio job running AI localisation
Save the extra salary on top of freelance income
Move part of her shares into AI companies

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2031. That's a real business cycle, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough to build something and short enough that you can't waste time. I'd tell younger translators to go to the studios now, not later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd get three years of very good money, because studios would need people who can run AI well before the AI runs itself. After 2031 the thinking work is gone, and that's all of my work, so it's about using the window.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a small localisation company with Priya and a friend who does audio, using AI for nearly everything and selling speed. I'd plan from day one to sell it or close it by 2030. And I'd put most of the profit into shares and maybe a small flat to rent out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but focused. Like a game with a timer on screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd plan to sell or close it. Why build it at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the next five years are where the money is, and I'd rather earn it as an owner than a freelancer. If I build it right, somebody bigger buys it in 2029. If not, I close it and keep the savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to you after 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know, and I'm not going to pretend. I'd have money, a bit of property, and I'd be 32. I'd figure it out from there.

I'd tell younger translators to join **the studios** now.
think: I'd get **three years** of very good money running AI for studios.
After **2031** all of my work is gone, so it's about using the window.

Put most of the profit into **shares and property**.

steps.text: Launch an AI localisation company with Priya and an audio friend

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Same ending, but loads of room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have a decade, so use it. Nobody needs to quit tomorrow, but nobody should be translating menus in 2035.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think this one's fine for me. I'd ride translation for five or six years, and still have time to land somewhere new by 35. The robot gap doesn't matter much for me, but the time does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend two or three years living in Tokyo, working with game studios there, building relationships that AI can't. I'd keep my freelance clients from there. Then in the second half of the decade I'd move into producing, managing the people and schedule of a game, if anything human is left in that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, mostly excited. It feels like a long stretch of road with a clear view.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why Tokyo specifically?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've only ever been there on holiday, and I've translated Japanese for six years. Being in the room with game studios matters more once the words themselves become cheap. Also, I'm young, I'd go now if I didn't have the rental lease.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is producing safe from AGI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, probably not by 2036. I'd be honest about that. But it puts me around people, and if anything human survives in games, it'll be closer to the people than the text.

The robot gap matters little to me, but **the time** does.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Not because I'd starve, but because I'd have to make the biggest decisions of my life in about a year. What would help is clear warning signs from governments, not just company press releases, so people can tell which picture we're in.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Whether players care. I think a lot of players would quietly accept a machine translation if it's free and comes out the same day as Japan. That's the part that scares me more than the technology.

headlineQuote: A lot of players would quietly accept a machine translation if it's free and comes out the same day as Japan.
portrait: Zoe is a 27-year-old **game localisation** translator, Japanese into English, living alone in a rented studio.
She **uses AI daily** and built her own translation pipeline, which makes her fast.
She has **ten months saved** plus shares, and low costs.
She stays **calm to anxious** across scenarios, never alarmed.
Her moves are bold: **sell her setup**, start a company, even move to Tokyo.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries her most, because huge decisions would land within a year.
whatWouldHelp: **Clear warning signs** from governments, not just company press releases.
